raw_case_text: A 76-year-old man was admitted to the emergency room after being found disoriented by his family. He experienced episodes of fever (38-39.5  C) in previous days. There were no other complaints including headache or seizures. His prior history included an HIV-1 infection diagnosed 10 years before, pulmonary tuberculosis, hypertension and hyperthyroidism. His medications included zidovudine, lamivudine, efavirenz, tiamazol, and captopril. The last laboratorial results showed a CD4 cell count of 668 cells/mm and HIV viral load < 50 copies/mL. At admission, the physical examination showed a patient in good general conditions, moderately dehydrated and pale, afebrile, and hemodynamically stable. The neurological exam showed disorientation in time and space with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 14. The rest of the examination was normal. Laboratorial tests showed leukocytosis with left shift and no other alterations. A brain computed tomography scan showed a single low attenuation lesion with a uniform ring enhancement in the left temporal region (Fig. 1A). At this moment, empiric treatment for toxoplasmosis with parenteral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (5/ 25 mg/ kg twice a day) was initiated. Seven days later, the patient's level of consciousness worsened, presenting disorientation and confusion. At this moment, after a review of the prior images, the hypothesis of bacterial or mycobacterial brain abscess was considered and ceftriaxone (2 g twice a day) and metronidazole (500 mg three times a day) were started. A lumbar puncture showed 1 cell/dL, 56 mg/dL of glucose, and 40 mg/dL of proteins. The cerebrospinal fluid direct exam and bacteria, fungus and mycobacteria cultures were all negative. The latex agglutination test for Cryptococcus neoformans,Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitides andHaemophylus influenzae type B, and the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for these bacteria as well as for Mycobacterium tuberculosis were also all negative. Blood cultures performed by automated microbiology growth and detection system for aerobic, anaerobic and fungi resulted negative. The patient underwent trepanation, and drainage of the lesion was performed. Purulent material was obtained and sent to culture, which resulted in the growth of methicillin-sensitive S. aureus. Anti-Toxoplasma treatment was discontinued and antibiotic scheme was changed to oxacillin (2 g six times a day). The patient received eight weeks of this medication, improved progressively, clinically and radiologically (Fig. 1B-C) and was discharged to home. The patient underwent dental examination, with no evidence of dental infection. At transesophageal echocardiography the valves and left atrium were free of thrombi and vegetations, and there was no evidence of infection in thechest radiography and also in the abdominal ultrasound. In the daily assessment, measures of capillary glycemia were normal. Despite intensive efforts, no predisposing condition leading to the brain abscess, including trauma or surgery, intravenous drug use, skin or soft tissue infection, empyema, lung or intraabdominal abscess, bacterial endocarditis, dental infection, sinusitis or mastoiditis, were identified.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 76-year-old HIV-positive man was brought to the emergency room after being found disoriented by his family following several days of fever (38.0–39.5 °C).
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the days preceding emergency room admission, the patient experienced intermittent fevers ranging from 38.0 to 39.5 °C before being discovered disoriented in time and space by family members.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV-1 infection diagnosed 10 years prior (well controlled with most recent CD4+ count 668 cells/mm3 and HIV viral load <50 copies/mL); previously treated pulmonary tuberculosis; hypertension; hyperthyroidism. No history of trauma, surgery, intravenous drug use, endocarditis, dental infection, sinusitis, or mastoiditis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for recent fevers (38.0–39.5 °C) and acute disorientation; negative for headache or seizures. Home medications: zidovudine, lamivudine, efavirenz, thiamazole (methimazole), and captopril.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, moderately dehydrated and pale, afebrile, and hemodynamically stable in good general condition. Neurological examination revealed disorientation to time and place with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 14 and no focal motor deficits. Dental examination was normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission blood tests showed leukocytosis with a left shift and normal daily capillary blood glucose. Automated aerobic, anaerobic, and fungal blood cultures were negative. Chest X-ray and abdominal ultrasound were normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Baseline CD4+ T-cell count was 668 cells/mm3. Brain CT demonstrated a solitary low-attenuation lesion with uniform ring enhancement in the left temporal lobe. Lumbar puncture CSF analysis showed 1 cell/dL, glucose 56 mg/dL, protein 40 mg/dL, and negative Gram/AFB/fungal stains, cultures, latex agglutination, and PCRs for Cryptococcus neoformans, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) showed normal valves and left atrium without vegetations or thrombi. Following surgical trepanation and abscess drainage on day 7, purulent aspirate culture grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Cryptogenic solitary left temporal lobe methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) brain abscess in a 76-year-old man with virologically suppressed HIV-1 infection (plasma HIV viral load <50 copies/mL, CD4+ count 668 cells/mm3 on zidovudine, lamivudine, and efavirenz). Initial empiric parenteral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (5/25 mg/kg BID) for presumed cerebral toxoplasmosis, followed on day 7 by empiric ceftriaxone (2 g BID) and metronidazole (500 mg TID) for worsening confusion, were replaced after neurosurgical trepanation and drainage isolated MSSA by an 8-week course of intravenous oxacillin (2 g six times daily), resulting in complete clinical and radiological resolution.
